What the claim means

Define “PFAS-free” before selecting a paper

PFAS is a broad group of substances, and market rules or customer protocols may use different definitions, methods and reporting thresholds. A useful sourcing program begins with the intended claim and the finished product—not a blanket statement about every paper item.

Intended use

Record the food type, temperature, contact time, baking or cooking conditions and expected grease or moisture performance.

Product construction

Identify the base paper, coating or treatment, ink system, adhesive where relevant, forming process and finished format.

Market protocol

Confirm the destination market, buyer restricted-substance requirements, test method and acceptable reporting threshold.

Documents and testing

Connect each document to the sample it represents

Available evidence may include a supplier statement, material declaration or third-party report. Buyers should check the issuer, date, test method, analyte scope, reporting limit, sample description and relationship to the finished product.

If the selected construction is not adequately represented, product-specific testing can be discussed before the commercial claim or packaging statement is finalized.

FAQ

PFAS-free baking paper FAQ

Does PFAS-free mean the same thing in every market?

No. Definitions, thresholds and buyer protocols can differ. The intended claim, destination market, product construction and agreed test method should be confirmed before approval.

Which products can use PFAS-free material options?

Applicable options can be discussed for baking cups, cupcake liners, baking parchment, air fryer paper liners, custom printed baking paper and selected greaseproof or food wrapping paper constructions. Availability depends on the paper, coating, ink, converting method and performance requirement.

What evidence can buyers request?

Depending on the selected material and order, buyers can request available supplier declarations, material statements or product-specific third-party test evidence. Every document should be checked against the exact tested sample and current specification.

Can one report cover every product?

Not automatically. A report only supports the tested or clearly represented construction. Changes in paper, coating, ink, supplier or manufacturing route may require a new technical review or additional testing.

How are repeat orders controlled?

The approved specification, material identity, artwork and supporting evidence should remain linked to the order. Material or supplier changes that may affect the claim should be reviewed before production.
